problems.title: Feasibility stopping does not certify the CAD projection
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1; Appendix C.1, PDF pp. 24–25 (arXiv v1 pp. 17–18).
claim: Appendix C.1, PDF pp. 24–25 (arXiv v1 pp. 17–18), explains stopping when \(\max_i(Ax^{(k)}-b)_i\le\epsilon\). Paraphrase preserving the qualification: the authors numerically observed that \(\|x-x^{(k)}\|_2\) is strictly increasing; assuming that observation holds generally, feasibility at zero tolerance is treated as equivalent to reaching \(P_C(x)\). The discussion then proposes lower and upper bounds on \(\|x-P_C(x)\|_2\) using the current distance and a Hoffman feasibility bound. This is presented as an empirical observation with an explicitly conditional argument, not as a proved monotonicity theorem. Algorithm 1 implements the feasibility-based stopping rule.

The precise suspect inference is from small constraint residual to small error relative to the projection of the original input. Feasibility measures proximity to any point of \(C\). Projection additionally minimizes distance to that input. A feasible nonoptimal iterate separates the two properties.
analysis: Feasibility bounds distance to the feasible set, whereas projection minimizes distance from the original input. A concrete CAD instance uses \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\-1&2\\-1&-4\\3&-3\end{pmatrix}\), \(b=(1,4,1,2)^\top\), and \(x^{(0)}=(6,-4)^\top\). Its origin is strictly feasible, all coordinate degrees equal four, and its only recession direction is zero. The exact projection is \(z^*=(11/21,-1/7)\), certified by nonnegative multipliers \((34/147,0,0,703/441)^\top\) satisfying stationarity and complementary slackness.

For the paper's equal-degree parallel Dykstra recurrence, the historical exact-rational calculation gives its first feasible iterate at \(k=40\), approximately \[(0.5223756630,-0.1442116690)\], with projection error \(0.001972485\). The squared distance from the input falls from \(44.8715776762\) at iteration \(39\) to \(44.8714720330\) at iteration \(40\), contrary to the monotonicity premise. A fresh independent rational evaluation of the displayed recurrence confirms the iterate and residual; the KKT certificate states the comparison target directly.
result: Feasibility stopping alone does not provide the asserted projection-error certificate, and the conditional monotonicity premise fails on this bounded example. The asymptotic CAD convergence theorem is not refuted.
repair: Use feasible primal and nonnegative dual points with \(F(z)=\|z-x\|_2^2/2\) and \(d(\lambda)=\lambda^\top(Ax-b)-\|A^\top\lambda\|_2^2/2\). The gap gives \(\|z-P_C(x)\|_2\le\sqrt{2(F(z)-d(\lambda))}\); a feasibility residual alone does not.
problems.impact_rationale: The stopping rationale and proposed bounds fail on one bounded exact CAD trajectory; asymptotic convergence and historical runtime rankings are not refuted.

problems.title: Proposition 1’s exactness criterion needs a dimensionality qualification
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Proposition 1(2), PDF p. 7; proof in Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23.
claim: Proposition 1, part \(2\), Section 3.3, PDF p. 7, and its proof in Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23, assert the following equivalence. Paraphrase: for a polytope represented by nonredundant linear inequalities and a point where projection is differentiable, \(S(x)=J(x)\) if and only if \(x\) lies in the ambient interior of \(C\), or \(P_C(x)\) lies in the interior of all but one defining half-space. The statement does not explicitly require \(C\) to be full-dimensional.

The converse proof identifies a locally \((n-1)\)-dimensional boundary with exactly one active defining inequality. That inference requires additional geometric qualifications and fails for lower-dimensional polytopes represented by inequalities.
analysis: The bounded set \(C=\{(u,v):u\le0,-u\le0,v\le1,-v\le1\}=\{0\}\times[-1,1]\) has four individually nonredundant inequalities. Near \(x=(1,0)\), projection is \((u,v)\mapsto(0,v)\), so \(J(x)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\). The residual direction is \((1,0)\), giving the same surrogate \(S(x)=I-dd^\top\), despite two active inequalities and empty ambient interior. A dimensionality or representation-independent active-rank qualification is necessary.
result: The universal necessity statement omits a geometric qualification. This lower-dimensional example does not occur in a strictly feasible full-dimensional benchmark construction and does not refute the other surrogate properties.
repair: State full dimensionality and an irredundant facet representation, or outside the set use the representation-independent condition \(S(x)=J(x)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)=n-1\), at differentiability points.
problems.impact_rationale: The necessity direction omits lower-dimensional geometry; the strictly feasible benchmark domain and other surrogate properties survive.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The stated constraint generator does not guarantee bounded polytopes
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, PDF p. 24 (random constraint generator).
claim: Appendix B.2, PDF p. 24, describes a sparse matrix with nonzero rows, independently sampled unit-length columns, and \(b=u+As\) with \(u_i\sim U(0.1,1)\) and Gaussian \(s\). Paraphrase: the construction produces nonempty bounded polytopes and guarantees that a radius-\(0.1\) ball fits inside the feasible set. The positive offsets indeed make \(s\) strictly feasible. They do not constrain recession directions.
analysis: Take \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3/5&5/13\\4/5&12/13\end{pmatrix}\), \(u=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(b=u+As\). Both columns have norm one, every row is nonzero, and \(\det A=16/65\). Yet \(v=(-1,-1)\) satisfies \(Av=(-64/65,-112/65)^\top<0\), so \(s+tv\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\). The set is strictly feasible but unbounded.

Column normalization also does not guarantee a radius-\(0.1\) inscribed ball. In three dimensions, choose rows \(\pm(3/5,3/5,3/5)\) and \(\pm(\sqrt{14}/10)e_j\) for each axis, with offsets \(0.101\). Columns have norm one and the coordinate constraints make the set bounded, but the first row pair confines it to a slab of width \(2(0.101)/(3\sqrt3/5)\approx0.194375<0.2\). No radius-\(0.1\) ball can fit.
result: The generator's algebraic conditions establish strict feasibility, but do not guarantee boundedness or the stated inradius. No claim is made that the authors' stored experimental matrices actually had these defects.
repair: Enforce row margins \(u_i\ge0.1\|a_i\|_2\) and finite box constraints around the feasible center with half-widths at least \(0.1\). These conditions certify the ball and boundedness, but they change the generated instance distribution.
problems.impact_rationale: Strictly feasible unit-column constructions need not be bounded or have the stated inradius; actual stored benchmark incidence remains unknown.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Candidate factor-of-two discrepancy in the printed DCP update
problems.source_location: Appendix D.6, Eq. (D.1), PDF p. 27 (arXiv v1 p. 20).
claim: This item is not counted as a supported substantive error under the requested exclusion of typographical mistakes. Appendix D.6, equation (D.1), PDF p. 27 (arXiv v1 p. 20), decomposes \(Q=D-C\) and prints an update whose linear term contains \(Dx^{(k)}\). For the displayed quadratic objective \(F(z)=z^TDz-z^TCz+c^Tz\), differentiation gives \(2Dx^{(k)}\) when \(D\) is symmetric diagonal. The source code for this baseline was unavailable to this audit, so the executed baseline cannot be inferred from that line alone.
analysis: Differentiating \(z^\top Dz\) for symmetric \(D\) gives \(2Dz\). In the scalar case \(D=3\), \(C=2\), \(c=0\), feasible interval \([-1,1]\), and current point \(1/2\), the printed update maximizes \(3(1/2)z-2z^2\), yielding \(3/8\). The stated objective \(F(z)=z^2\) decreases from \(1/4\) to \(9/64\). The baseline source is unavailable, so this remains a literal-formula concern whose implementation impact is unresolved.
result: Literal-formula discrepancy supported; effect on the executed baseline remains unresolved and is not counted as an established empirical defect.
repair: The tangent update uses \(2Dx^{(k)}\); maximizing its touching global lower surrogate gives a nondecreasing objective. This local ascent property does not imply global nonconvex optimality.
problems.impact_rationale: The literal tangent factor differs, but an isolated display error and the unavailable executed baseline cannot be distinguished.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

impact_rationale: The latest accessible paper channels retain local stopping, geometric-domain and generator guarantee gaps. CAD convergence remains intact, and the candidate baseline formula issue lacks implementation evidence.
